doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

title: Is a jazz band a democracy? Leadership and Mulligan
summary: Poston says a band needs a leader, as Mulligan insisted, and describes having to lead the bands he assembled.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Okay. All right here’s a little scenario. I’m a guest speaker at a symposium, a jazz symposium, and you’re in the audience and I come out and one of the things I say is, “A jazz band is the embodiment of an unfettered democracy.”
Well I agree. I agree with that. I’ve heard Wynton say that many times and I think it’s — I mean you’re talking it just being a democratic process.

I am but I’m also quoting from a review on your Gerry Mulligan book and it said for one Mulligan took the managerial aspect of being a bandleader seriously. His approach pours cold water on the romantic ideal that a jazz band is about unfettered democracy.

I could very much speak to that from personal experience in many of these things. It truly is a case by case, band by band kind of a thing. There has to be a leader. Gerry was always very specific and he’s absolutely a thousand percent right, there has to be a leader. So it’s a democratic process when they are actually playing together, because then that role isn’t required. I mean you know then it’s a process where they’re creating music together and everyone has a role that they can take liberties with as needed and so on and so forth, unless it’s a chart that you’re playing necessarily, but even within that there’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

interpretations. But even for what I do, and I learned very early on of having to put different bands together and create different things. You can’t just usually put a band together and hope that — and say, “Okay we want you to play — we want you to do a tribute to Jazz at the Philharmonic and we want you to do a Jazz at the Philharmonic type concert” because there’ll be a lot of standing around and either one of two things will happen. Either one person that’s a Gerry Mulligan type will just step forward and start to take the reins and say okay well I think we should start with “I Got Rhythm,” or there’ll be a lot of standing around and not knowing what to do depending on who the participants are. So I had to learn through the years, sometimes the hard way, that sometimes that had to be me and that was hard for me to do because I had such — I was so much younger than the other people and I had so much respect for those guys that I never saw myself as someone who should be telling those guys what to do. But then you learn as you go that in certain cases you’re ultimately responsible for it and you’ve got to make sure that what you want to have happen happens. So you either appoint a leader that’s somebody who will do it, or you have to at least assume some of that role yourself. I would always obviously try to appoint a leader, but sometimes you would have to step in and do that. So yes, Gerry was not a guy — Gerry was very much a leader. And I think that’s one of his attributes is the fact that Gerry had a vision and Gerry knew what he wanted and he knew how to get it and he had no problem being the leader. And that’s the thing you know Gerry would say, and it’s in the book you know it can’t be a democracy. Well what he’s talking about is that type of scenario. Now when Gerry would walk out unannounced at the Newport Jazz Festival to just participate in one of the jam sessions that he loved to do that might have been him and Coleman Hawkins and Ben Webster and whoever, then it’s more of what we’re talking about as a democratic process of those guys are playing together and there nobody is saying you only take two choruses, you know I mean there’s more of a given — you know there’s more of that process. So I think there’s two sides to it and it depends on the circumstances and what you’re doing. But I noticed that even from having to, you know a lot of things I’ve done there has to be rehearsals obviously, if you’re doing big band concerts where you’re reading, there has to be rehearsals to some degree. And I would always use, if I could, ‘cause it was more appealing to me personally but it was also more of a selling point to the audience, like for example if you’re doing a Stan Kenton alumni event playing Pete Rugolo’s music and Pete Rugolo’s the guy conducting the band, that’s a big deal. But now Pete was not very comfortable in that role. Pete was very shy. Pete didn’t like — Pete wasn’t loud, he wasn’t demanding. Pete would conduct but he just kind of expected everybody would do their job and he wouldn’t have to discipline anybody or this, that or the other.
